narrative:
The model estimated a 56.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is slightly more likely than passing, and because your law school application was tied to this prediction, it was denied. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty.

The strongest reason was your third-year academic standing. Your third-year decile was 2, compared with an average of about 5.8 among accepted students, and this was the most influential factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor. At 3.30, it was slightly above the accepted-student average of 3.23, so it pushed toward passing and worked in your favor, but it was not enough to outweigh the concern about your later law-school grades. Your family income bracket, upper-middle, was the third most influential factor and pushed toward failure in your case. Gender and race were not used in the prediction.

To improve your chances, ask admissions for specific feedback, consider additional academic work or a post-baccalaureate program that demonstrates readiness, and prepare early for bar-related subjects. If the school allows it, explain any circumstances behind your third-year grades and show an upward trend. Reapplying with stronger evidence of academic performance is the most direct path.
